I guess you don't like Star Trek for the same reason ;-)

"Going the way of the dodo" quite literally means going extinct because white Western European interlopers. The Wikipedia page is an interesting read. Dodos were friendly and fearless; Dutch sailors learned they could walk up to one, grab it by the leg, and its resulting screams would draw out all the other dodos in the area to assist, who would be captured as well.

This same class of people utilized/ rationalized slavery and practiced/ rationalized genocide on both sides of the Atlantic. Speaking for myself as a member of this class, this SCP is extremely important to me and for the health of the Foundation, in and out of the Foundation universe. It made me profoundly uncomfortable to be inconveniently reminded of this atrocity in the middle of my late-night escape from the real world: how dare you make me feel something, and thereby make me think about why I felt.

(What better compliment to a writer could there be, other than "you made me feel and think"?! (OK, I +1'd this as well.))

One such as myself may wish not to be reminded of the atrocities of the past (which I today benefit from). I might also wish for a world where humans are no longer tribal (in the sense of, "you're different than me, and therefore inferior"). Wouldn't it be a dream world where bringing up slavery, Trail of Tears, Auschwitz, and yes the dodo would be so foreign to the human DNA as to warrant an eye-roll? Until then, please keep writing and keep reminding me!

I think it's deeper than that, that anomalies are about perception and what is deemed "proper". Pre-Emancipation (even post-Emancipation) non-white races (beyond African American slaves, this included other groups like the Irish and Asians) were seen as inferior to whites, and even in the free states this was not an uncommon opinion. So, to someone with that opinion, a non-white person saying they are equal to a white person is "abnormal", and rare cases of abnormality are anomalies.

The ASCI was, of course, wrong and, of course, they thought they were "right". The Foundation does what it believes is right (even many times taking cruel actions of the few for the sake of the many, beyond D-Class) but it could be revealed that certainly anomalies never needed such testing.

It can also make one wonder if some of the more minor skips (especially those that are "safe") shouldn't be thought of as anomalies at all.

item.content:encoded:
Ever hear of J. Marion Sims?

Scientist and physician, known as the 'father of American gynecology'. Discovered a way to surgically repair fistulas, invented a new type of speculum, etc etc etc. Brilliant, brilliant man. Advanced the practice of medicine greatly.

Used slave women as experimental subjects. Did lots of 'practice surgery' on them until he figured out what he was doing wrong. Would he have used anesthetic on them if anesthetic were more readily available at that time? No way to know. Also did experiments on slave infants - if you mutilate their skull bones like this, does that cause trismus? What about if you mutilate their skull bones like that ?

Sims was an educated man. He knew the truth. He was dedicated to the scientific method and the advancement of human knowledge.

And look what he did.

This actually happened, AlysonSkye. In 1851, Samuel Cartwright actually made a presentation to the Medical Association of Louisiana, describing a mental illness which caused slaves to flee slavery. And he actually called it "drapetomania". Cartwright was a scientist too — he made several advances in the field of public health, leading to considerable improvements in the sanitary conditions in Confederate army camps. As well, he did a lot of important research into yellow fever and cholera.

And not only did he say that slaves were susceptible to a mental illness that made them want to be free, he also said that they were susceptible to a kind of pathological laziness (which was far more prevalent in free blacks than in slaves, so obviously it was better for them to remain slaves). One of the "symptoms" of this pathological laziness was lessened skin sensitivity, which meant that whipping was "therapeutic".

The only difference between this story and reality is that, in a universe where there were anomalies in need of containment and an American Secure Containment Initiative to contain them, Cartwright joined the Initiative and secretly proposed drapetomania as something anomalous instead of publicly presenting it as a medical phenomenon of unknown etiology.

item.content:encoded:
I think you have somewhat missed the point. The implications of "A Doctor Said So" is really at the core of this. The general and under-educated tend to believe and accept what 'educated' men have to say. Just as most today will accept what is stated on the news, being delivered to us by 'experts'. Many highly toxic medications were prescribed by legitimate doctors throughout the years. Psychology studies show that people are more likely to be obedient to someone in a labcoat, whether or not the person is actually an expert or not. Remember, the world was flat until a few hundred years ago.

It is not a matter of people being stupid. It is a matter of public perception. As was mentioned in a previous post, many of the new industries of the North (at the time) did not care about slaves' rights, they merely kept in line with the government. The ASCI was a group of Southern gentlemen, who were investigators of the anomalous. Being a 'new disease' proposed by the general scientific community, it required further investigation. Since this anomaly could be understood and catalogued (causes of susceptibility, fairly specific effects), this group had a file on it.

As for your example of a 'SCP that causes homosexuality', there are still groups today that believe it is a genetic defect. Popular opinion of the natural/unnatural status of it has varied widely by culture throughout history. I also vaguely recollect that object existing as an SCP.

What makes this horrifying is the fact that though that concept is ridiculous today, it was a perfectly reasonable explanation of a growing 'problem' then. That and taking baths in radium water to loosen your back, swallowing a ball of silver to unclog the bowels, and many, many other examples of bad science. The fact that the general population will so easily fall prey to this is what is REALLY scary. This is quite real and personally, scares the crap out of me.

Oh, and +1. Excellently written, seriously creepy. Gonna be pondering this one for weeks.

item.content:encoded:
This just barely works for me. The fact that it's not a SCP Foundation document originally, but was apparently picked up somewhere along the line by the organization in the 19 century, takes some of the annoying factor away for me.

I would really like to see others' reservations addressed, particularly yoric's and Sorts'.

Specifically, re Sorts' complaint, I'd like to see something that takes this away from the implied "we used to believe this, but then we discovered that racism is bad, so we stopped." Sure that sounds nice, but it's not really horrifying and doesn't say anything interesting.

And I see you addressed yoric's complaint, but from where I'm standing you did it in the wrong way.

Tell Cartwright he can go to hell. We'll remove it, but we're keeping a record of what we've done. His family did this, and we helped him; we're not whitewashing the record for him. I don't know how we'll ever make up for what we've done here, but the least we can do is remember. O5-9

Get rid of that or rewrite it.

I mean, I agree with the sentiments expressed there, and in an ideal world an O5 would write that. But I don't believe that they would, especially not in 1916, and I think the fact that we're making reparations says that at least some people in the Foundation felt guilty. But I bet others did not. Not to put too fine a point on it, but this is like writing a historical document that indicates that the sole reason for the Civil War was to free the slaves, when it was at least in some part motivated by economic factors of the time. Prettying up history gets no points from me. (no one call it 'whitewashing' pretty please okay :P)

Also, yes, it's possible to come up with an explanation for why the O5 wrote that, but I'm not buying it until the article itself sells it to me, because it's that awful combination of 'cliche' and 'unlikely'.

There's something else that bugs me here, but I can't quite put my finger on it - may be my own background, but if I can clarify I'll let you know.

However, due to how well-written most of the article is, how plausible/believable it is, how horrified I am and have always been by drapetomania, and how pleased I am that someone's using Actual Less-Well-Known Historical Stuff in an SCP article, I'm still upvoting this. But please take a look at the above issues anyway.

PS there is no reason on gods' green earth that we need a "drapetomania" tag, and I've removed it. :P (Yes I can do that, since I'm part of the Great Tagging Project. Fear me, or something.)

Why would the Foundation (or its forefathers) want that?
From their point of view it's just a psychological disease which can be cured by appropriate methods. It's not the first, it's not the last (search for "hysteria" on Wikipedia, for example). It's far too widespread to be contained. There's nothing really anomalous about it, it's a disease like any other.
Basically, it's just history wrapped in a thin SCP foil. And in my humble opinion, this one performs much worse than, let's say, "Conviction".

Some parts of this story are praiseworthy - the style, the "Drapetomaniac Class" and the footnotes. But the whole idea just doesn't feel like it.
